findings.title: Case-sensitive matching allows blocked addresses to bypass the ban
findings.body: Neither BlockedEmail creation nor this lookup normalizes the address. A block for `bad@spammers.org` therefore does not match `bad@SPAMMERS.ORG`, even though email domains are case-insensitive. A user can change the domain's capitalization to pass the new validation and register with the same blocked mailbox. Apply consistent email normalization when storing and looking up blocked addresses.

findings.title: Concurrent matches lose counter increments
findings.body: The read-modify-save sequence is not atomic. Two requests matching the same address can both read match_count as N and both save N+1, recording only one of the two matches. Concurrent registration attempts therefore undercount blocked-email activity. Increment the counter atomically in the database or protect the update with a row lock.

findings.title: Rejected user saves roll back the match statistics
findings.body: When this helper runs inside User.save or User.save!, the BlockedEmail save joins the enclosing user transaction. The email validator then adds a blocking error, causing Rails to roll back that transaction—including match_count and last_match_at. Paths such as User.create_for_email, which calls save! without a preceding standalone valid? call, reject the address without recording the match. Persist rejected-match statistics independently of the failed user transaction and cover this through a user-save integration test.
